div.p: Self-suspension introduces further complexity in the scheduling of real-time tasks. As a result, the proofs of optimality for the typical Earliest-Deadline-First (EDF) and Deadline-Monotonic (DM) scheduling do not hold. The EDF-Like scheduling algorithms allows to optimize the scheduling algorithm by setting relative priority points. In this work, we show that a tuning process of the relative priority points leads to significantly better (analytical) schedulability guarantees. Moreover, we discuss open problems and alternative approaches.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: In real-time systems, each job has to finish until its absolute deadline. This property is called schedulability of the system and has to be verified under a given scheduling algorithm using a related schedulability test. In the literature the schedulability under different scheduling algorithms has been analyzed. Liu and Layland [3] studied Deadline-Monotonic (DM) and Earliest-Deadline-First (EDF) scheduling for ordinary tasks. They showed that EDF is optimal (i.e., provides the best schedulability guarantees) and established that DM is optimal among Fixed-Priority (FP) scheduling algorithms. However, as soon as self-suspension is involved this does not hold anymore.

A job of a self-suspending task may release the processor before being completed, for instance when waiting to get access to a shared resource or offloading computation to an external device, and continue its execution later on. Under this setting, the proofs of [3] about the optimality for EDF and DM do not hold anymore, and there may potentially be better scheduling algorithms for self-suspending task sets.

In our earlier work [1] we provided a schedulabiltiy test under EDF-Like (EL) scheduling. EL scheduling was originally proposed by Leontyev and Anderson [2] and allows to set a task-specific priority point (PP) Π i which determines the job priorities of task τ i . By configuring the PP accordingly, a variety of different scheduling algorithms can be covered, including but not limited to DM and EDF. This leads to the question:

Can we find an EL scheduling algorithm that shows better schedulability than EDF and DM for self-suspending tasks? In the remainder of this work, we discuss possible optimization approaches and ideas. Specifically, our contributions are as follows.

Contribution: In this work we improve the schedulability of self-suspending tasks by optimizing the PP of EL schedul-ing. To that end we present a first optimization approach that tunes the PP for a given task set in Section III. Moreover, we discuss further optimization ideas and open research questions in Section IV.

div.head: II. SYSTEM MODEL
div.p: Let T = {τ 1 , . . . , τ n } be a set of n ∈ N self-suspending sporadic real-time tasks in a uniprocessor system. Each task τ i is described by a 4-tuple τ i = (C i , S i , D i , T i ), composed of worst-case execution time (WCET) C i ≥ 0, maximum suspension time S i ≥ 0, relative deadline D i ≥ 0, and minimum inter-arrival time T i > 0. Each task τ i releases an infinite number of jobs according to T i , i.e., two job releases are at least T i time units apart. We denote by r i,j the release of the j-th job τ i,j of τ i . Each job τ i,j must be executed for c i,j ∈ [0, C i ] time units until its absolute deadline d i,j = r i,j +D i . Each job may suspend itself dynamically, i.e., it may suspend itself as often as desired without exceeding the maximum suspension time S i . We denote by U i := Ci Ti the utilization of task τ i and by U := n i=1 U i the total utilization of the task set T.

In EDF-Like (EL) scheduling, the jobs are scheduled according to an absolute priority point π i,j ∈ R. More specifically, a job τ i,j has higher priority than τ i ,j if π i,j < π i ,j . The absolute PP is computed by adding the release of the job and a task specific parameter Π i denoted as relative priority point, i.e., π i,j = r i,j + Π i . Therefore, a smaller relative PP Π i in comparison to the other relative PPs favor jobs of τ i to be scheduled first. The left picture of Figure 1 depicts the notation. div.head: III. FIRST OPTIMIZATION APPROACH
div.p: Given a taskset we use the analysis from our earlier work [1] to obtain an upper bound R i on the worst-case response time (WCRT) of each task τ i . That is, each job τ i,j finishes until r i,j + R i . If R i ≤ D i for all i ∈ {1, . . . , n}, then the taskset is schedulable. However, if there exists an i ∈ {1, . . . , n} such that R i > D i , then the test cannot guarantee the schedulability of the system. In that case we can tune the relative PPs such that the task set becomes schedulable. During the evaluation of [1] we made the following observation. Whether this observation can be proven analytically or is just a trend still has to be discussed. In any case, we can utilize this observation for a tuning process, which consist of the following steps:
1) For all tasks τ i ∈ T, we set the relative PP to Π i = D i (configuration for typical EDF behavior). 2) If R i ≤ D i for all tasks, then the task set is schedulable.

3) Otherwise, let I be the set of all indices i ∈ {1, . . . , n} such that R i < D i . 4) Reduce the relative PP of all tasks τ i , i ∈ I by increasing the relative PP by D i -R i . That is, we set Π i := Π i + D i -R i for all i ∈ I. 5) Repeat steps 2)-4) until the task set is schedulable or a maximal number a of iterations is reached. Following this simple tuning approach with a maximal number of a = 200 iterations shows promising results: We generated 500 task sets for each utilization U = 0.1, 0.2, . . . , 1.0. Random WCETs were generated using the UUnifast algorithm and the suspension was randomly drawn from the interval [0, 0.5] • (T i -C i ) for each task τ i . For the experiment, the performance of EL scheduling using our tuning process (EL Optimized) was compared with the state-of-the-art analyses for EDF and DM scheduling. We evaluated the acceptance ratio, which is the number of schedulable task sets divided by the total number of task sets. The results are presented in Figure 2. We observe that EL scheduling with the tuned parameters clearly outperforms typical EDF and DM scheduling.

div.head: IV. FURTHER OPTIMIZATION IDEAS AND OPEN QUESTIONS
div.p: In the previous section we have shown the potential of parameter tuning when EL scheduling for self-suspending tasks is utilized. However, the analytical reasoning behind the tuning process is not fully developed yet. In particular, does Observation 1 always hold, and can we guarantee that the tuning process improves the schedulability? Even further, it is unclear if the optimization approach from the previous section only optimizes locally and or globally, i.e., is the approach dependent on the choice of the initial relative PP in Step 1)?

In Section III, we reduce the priority of all tasks τ i with R i < D i by increasing their relative PP by D i -R i . Instead, we could also increase the priority of all tasks with R i > D i by reducing their relative PP by R i -D i . First experiments for this approach seem to indicate that this technique overshoots the optimization goal since reducing the relative PP of τ i makes some tasks τ j = τ i unschedulable which have WCRT R j close to their deadline D j .
Machine learning might be utilized to generate relative PPs Π i for EL scheduling. However, generating a set of relative PPs independent of the number of tasks in the task set is challenging.

V. CONCLUSION When self-suspension is considered, there may be scheduling algorithms with better schedulability guarantees than EDF and DM. In this work, we consider EDF-Like (EL) scheduling and provide a simple optimization approach to tune the relative priority points for EL scheduling. This tuning increases the schedulability significantly and motivates further exploration of different approaches to optimize the parameters of EL scheduling.
